extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, and theatre students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for teaching/performing improvisation games (especially 'What Comes Next') and for using status exercises to create character and story. Covers story structure (platform, trouble, endings), audience/committee feedback, exercises, and specific high/low status behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a platform
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish both a hero and what normality is like for that hero; provide the story's initial context (platform) so that middles and endings depend on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Building platforms doesn’t just mean delaying trouble until we’ve gotten to know the hero a bit. All of the arbitrary details later become 'good ideas'—you just have to remember to use them." Use platform details later for reincorporation; avoid retrospective platform-building where possible because it risks deus ex machina endings. Examples: trowel, apron, car gadgets introduced early so their later use satisfies audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break the routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a break in the normal routine early to signal the start of story development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking routines feels like the start of a story and typically happens early. The break should create momentum toward trouble rather than disperse it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get into trouble
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the hero into 'the right trouble'—a source of conflict that follows naturally from the platform and feels appropriate to the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'trouble salad' (trouble from multiple unrelated sources) and unrelated obstacles. The trouble should be credible for the hero and provide opportunities to raise stakes and force moral choices. Example progression: platform → prick finger (weak) → rose dies (needs justification) → boss sees you (payoff). Once you have the right trouble, stop adding new unrelated ideas; develop it instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise the stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously escalate consequences rather than resolving or lowering them; keep audience investment high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not solve problems prematurely (e.g., quick apology that cancels stakes). If performers start to 'solve' the problem, remind them to raise stakes or choose a different plan that increases tension. Raising stakes helps sustain interest and leads to satisfying middles and endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reincorporate previous elements to create endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use elements introduced in the platform (reincorporation) to provide structure and satisfying endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reincorporation prevents deus ex machina and gives the ending a sense of inevitability. Teach exercises that encourage remembering and reusing platform details. Example: the rose hidden under the shirt leading to being stabbed by a thorn. In rehearsal/post-show audit, ask 'What elements do we have in the platform?' and use them for endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deus ex machina/retrospective platform-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of inventing new elements late to resolve conflict; these can feel like cheats to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrospective platform-building is possible but harder to get right and risks unsatisfying endings. Instead, introduce necessary capabilities and items earlier so their later use feels earned (example: Q explaining Aston Martin gadgets in Goldfinger so the audience remembers them when used).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right trouble for the right hero (avoid 'trouble salad')
rubrics_metrics.description: Match the nature and source of trouble to who the hero is; trouble should feel 'right' and come from a source suggested by the platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If trouble comes from multiple, unconnected sources, it will feel wrong. Know your hero early—once you know who they are, it's far easier to deliver the right trouble and then stop adding new unrelated ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not solve problems too soon (preserve dramatic tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid choices or actions that prematurely cancel the stakes and reduce audience engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of anti-patterns: characters apologizing and having the other accept, hiding actions that undo being seen. Instead, let complications deepen (e.g., hiding a rose under a shirt leads to thorn injury) and maintain moral choices for the hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-improv analysis / auditing scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: After a show, analyze scenes to identify missing structural elements (e.g., platforms, break of routine, raised stakes, reincorporations) and use that to guide future practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analysis to establish a syllabus for improvement: e.g., 'We’re really lacking platforms—next show, positive platforms.' Learning to audit scenes lets groups correct persistent bad habits and plan concrete exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'What Comes Next' game mechanics and learning aims
rubrics_metrics.description: 'What Comes Next' is a theoretical game to teach story-building: players supply successive suggestions that build platform, break routine, and create trouble; players must learn to trust 'obvious' ideas and to develop stories from prompts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use variants: single-suggestion play, committees, random-word insertion, chapter-joining (A provides platform, B justifies connection). Caveats: random-word insertion keeps stories moving but can lead to stories that never end; the game is a learning tool and analysis method, not a performance technique to be overused. Teach both roles so everyone experiences being the suggester and the responder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and committee responsibility (yays/boos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience (or a small committee) must give honest feedback (yays/boos) to guide improvisers; the feedback-givers are responsible for quality control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If playing 'What Comes Next' with a committee (about three people between audience and actor), only committee members answer and the audience still reacts. Majority boos can force substitution. Remind committee members they are 'dependent on the yays and the boos'—if improvisers 'crash' it's the audience/committee's fault for not guiding them. Ask committees for a series of six to eight suggestions to reduce pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach both instinctive and intellectual approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine instinct-focused exercises (e.g., Word At A Time) and structure-focused exercises (e.g., What Comes Next) early in training to cater to different learning styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thinkers/planners will enjoy structure and analysis; doers/feelers will prefer plunging in. Teaching both helps each group develop underused skills: thinkers need to feel more, feelers need to think more. Don’t substitute analysis for inspiration; theory is a learning tool, not a live-scene diagnostic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-analysis during live scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not analyze a scene in progress; pausing to apply theoretical analysis will disrupt performance and miss spontaneous material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical analysis is valuable for post-show learning, but only a minority of improvisers can analyze in real time without missing dialogue. Use theory to retune instincts, not to replace them during scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status is conveyed primarily by behavior, not dialogue or social markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Status is what observers guess about another’s power/control based on behavior; it has less to do with class, job, accent, or dress and more to do with physicality and micro-behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If body and dialogue are incongruent, the body will tend to 'win.' Status cues are often subconscious but convey a great deal of information quickly. Teaching status early helps performers create richer characters and believable interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach status early in improv training
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce status exercises early because they help students focus on story, characters, and believable interaction and reduce anxiety about performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status requires people to maintain behaviors, leaving less mental space to worry about story/failure. Status exercises are practical ways to get students improvising after theoretical work like 'What Comes Next.'

rubrics_metrics.name: High status behaviors (practical checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete behaviors that reliably signal higher status in performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the text: "To Be More High Status …" with items: Gesture infrequently but purposefully; Make the middle of your body (throat to belt) bigger and taller; Enter someone else’s personal space; Speak in very short sentences; Pause and comfortably sustain the silence; Hold eye contact; React minimally to the physical presence of others; Place your feet a little wider apart than normal and then don’t move them for a while; Think about touching the other person’s head (but don’t do it!). Use these specific behaviors rather than relying on status signifiers like wealth or title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low status behaviors (practical checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete behaviors that reliably signal lower status in performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the text: "To Be More Low Status …" with items: Touch your face nervously and intermittently; Use long rambling sentences, fragmenting your speech; Make the middle of your body smaller; Try to keep a distance from other people; Want to look at others but hate to make eye contact; Giggle nervously; Shift from foot to foot or make other purposeless repetitive movements with your hands; Answer quickly and say 'er' before you speak; Put your feet very close together, perhaps with one foot crossed over the other. These behaviors are more effective than labeling a character as 'poor' or 'wealthy'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 'still head' and eye-contact exercises to create high/low status contrasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical exercise: have performers do the same lines twice—first with low-status physicality (fidgets, looking away), then with a still head and sustained eye contact to produce high-status reading of identical dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The group will perceive the first as 'awkward/anxious' and the second as 'sexy/confident/intimidating' even with similar dialogue. The 'still head' tends to reduce filler words and unnecessary gestures and produces cluster effects that reinforce status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status behaviours cluster and are individualized
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing one physical aspect (e.g., still head) will often unconsciously change other behaviors (fewer 'ers', longer pauses) and different triggers work differently on different people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should help performers discover which status triggers are strong/weak for them personally (e.g., folding arms may not read high status for everyone). Work experimentally to find truthful behaviors at any point on the status spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual nature of status (off-stage and stakes-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Status relationships vary by context and stakes: high-stakes environments (military, hospitals, fast-pace kitchens) widen status gaps; titles and rituals often formalize status but individual perception matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to create interesting character dynamics (e.g., high-status janitor vs low-status managing director). Be aware that societal markers (titles) can be status-levelers or levelers (e.g., informal 'Call me Bob'). Exploit status incongruities to refresh well-known roles.
